section_1.title: Introduction: The Geometry of a Sliced Cone
section_1.content: Briefly define a cone and show how slicing it at different angles creates various shapes: circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas. Introduce the 'Dandelin Spheres' as the geometric 'Rosetta Stone' that explains why these shapes share the same algebraic properties.
section_1.example: Visual: A virtual flashlight beam hitting a wall, changing shape as the angle of the wall tilts relative to the beam.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Concept: Tangency and Focus
section_2.content: Define the relationship between a sphere and a plane. Key takeaway: Any two tangent lines from a point to a sphere are equal in length. This is the hidden key that bridges the sphere to the conic section.
section_2.example: A marble (sphere) touching a glass plate (plane) at exactly one point.

section_3.title: The Dandelin Construction
section_3.content: Animate the process: Place a sphere inside a cone such that it is tangent to both the cone (along a circle) and the slicing plane (at a point F). This point F is the 'focus' of our conic section.
section_3.example: An animation of a translucent cone with a glowing sphere inside, showing the point of tangency F appearing on the cut surface.

section_4.title: Proving the Ellipse Property
section_4.content: Demonstrate that for any point P on the ellipse, the sum of distances to the two foci (PF1 + PF2) is constant. Use the property that segments tangent to the same sphere are equal to prove the distance sum equals the distance between the two circles of tangency.
section_4.example: A robotic arm tracing the perimeter of an ellipse, while two lines are drawn from the pen to the two 'hidden' foci, showing their sum remains constant.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Real-world Application
section_5.content: Summarize how this bridge between 3D solids and 2D curves provides a unified vision of geometry. Mention applications in optics (satellite dishes) and orbital mechanics.
section_5.example: A satellite dish (parabola) or a comet's orbit around the sun (ellipse), visualized through the lens of the cone-sphere intersection.
